cardio-chest-pressure.S:
CC: Exertional chest pressure, 3 weeks.
HPI: 30-year-old woman with progressive substernal pressure, now triggered by one flight of stairs instead of heavier exertion. Episodes last about 5 minutes, 6/10, radiate to left arm/jaw and resolve with rest. Associated dyspnea, sweating and nausea. No rest pain, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, PND or edema. Not pleuritic, positional or meal-related; antacids ineffective. No similar prior episodes. Worried about her heart and about missing work.
PMH: HTN, familial hypercholesterolemia, prediabetes. PSH: Appendectomy at 20; no subsequent admission.
Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; no aspirin. NKDA.
SH: Warehouse supervisor; smokes 1 pack/day since 18; 2–3 beers most evenings; no recreational drugs. Little exercise; frequent takeout.
FH: Father died of MI at 41; mother has HTN/diabetes; brother has inherited high cholesterol.
ROS: CV as above. Respiratory: no cough, hemoptysis or wheeze. GI: nausea; no heartburn, vomiting or abdominal pain. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
P: 1. Arrange EMS transfer now; obtain ECG promptly and serial troponin through the emergency team without delaying transfer. Review allergy, bleeding and hemodynamics before clinician-directed aspirin/anti-ischemic therapy. Explain the worsening exertional pattern, avoid exertion and do not drive; defer stress testing and OMT until ACS is excluded.

2. Obtain echocardiography with Doppler if valve disease remains suspected; cardiology review alongside the ischemia assessment. Avoid heavy exertion pending assessment; explain to report faintness or worsening dyspnea immediately.

3. After urgent causes are excluded, review reflux symptoms and consider an acid-suppression trial; counsel on tobacco cessation and avoiding late meals. Arrange primary-care follow-up after emergency assessment; antacid relief would not exclude ischemia.

gi-epigastric-melena.S:
CC: Burning epigastric pain, 6 weeks; worse for 3 days.
HPI: 29-year-old woman with nonradiating burning/gnawing pain, 7/10 worst and 3/10 between episodes. Worse fasting, at night, with coffee and greater ibuprofen use; brief relief with food/antacids. One black tarry stool 2 days ago; started borrowed iron 1 week ago. Nausea, fatigue for 2–3 weeks and lightheadedness on standing. No hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, weight loss, dysphagia, jaundice, fever or diarrhea. No prior ulcer. Worried about gastric cancer.
PMH: Chronic knee pain after sports injuries; migraines. PSH: Cholecystectomy at 25; two vaginal deliveries.
Meds: Ibuprofen 800 mg 2–3 times/day for months; ferrous sulfate for 1 week; no PPI. Penicillin causes lip/facial swelling.
SH: School administrator; husband and two children; no tobacco/drugs; 1–2 glasses wine on weekends. FH: Mother died of gastric cancer at 68; father has HTN; sister healthy.
ROS: GI as above; no vomiting. General: fatigue, no fever, night sweats or weight loss. Hematologic: lightheadedness and reported pallor, no bruising, gum bleeding or epistaxis. LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy not suspected, not tested.
P: 1. Arrange emergency evaluation today for suspected upper-GI bleeding; obtain CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation studies and type/screen, with resuscitation as indicated and GI consultation/endoscopy after stabilization. Stop ibuprofen; clinician-directed acid suppression and alternative analgesia. Explain black tarry stools, hematemesis and syncope as urgent warnings; immediate disposition replaces routine follow-up.

2. GI evaluation and appropriate biopsy at endoscopy if a lesion is identified; investigate H. pylori and tailor treatment to results and penicillin allergy. Explain the purpose of tissue diagnosis and arrange specialist follow-up based on the actual findings.

3. Obtain ferritin, iron studies and reticulocyte count; trend hemoglobin during evaluation. Discuss iron replacement after stabilization and source assessment. Explain that anemia may contribute to fatigue/faintness; defer OMT during acute bleeding.

neuro-thunderclap-headache.S:
CC: Sudden severe headache, 6 hours.
HPI: 28-year-old woman with occipital pain radiating to neck, maximal within 1 minute while lifting, 10/10 and constant. Unlike her usual gradually developing unilateral migraine. Sumatriptan 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg ineffective; light, bending and cough worsen pain. Neck stiffness, two vomiting episodes and transient greying of vision without a fall. No focal weakness, numbness, speech change, persistent visual change, seizure, fever, rash, head trauma. Worried about ruptured aneurysm.
PMH: Migraines since 17; no HTN. PSH/admissions: None.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN, ibuprofen 800 mg PRN, oral contraceptive daily. NKDA.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband; 0.5 pack/day for 8 years; wine a few times/week; no illicit drugs. LMP 2 weeks ago; reports pregnancy unlikely.
FH: Mother survived ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49; father and brother well.
ROS: Neurologic as above; no seizure or focal deficit reported. HEENT: photophobia/neck stiffness, no diplopia or persistent visual change. General: vomiting; no fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss.
P: 1. Immediate EMS transfer for noncontrast head CT and emergency specialist assessment; do not drive. Further testing after a negative CT depends on onset time, image quality and residual suspicion; discuss LP/vascular imaging with the emergency team. Explain that thunderclap onset requires urgent care despite preserved function.

2. Assess infection features; obtain appropriate blood/CSF studies through the emergency team when safe. Do not delay empiric therapy if bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected. Explain deterioration warnings and involve the husband in the immediate care plan.

3. Consider brain MRI after the emergency evaluation if a structural lesion remains plausible; neurology consultation and clinician-directed analgesia. Explain uncertainty and arrange follow-up. Defer cervical manipulation pending exclusion of urgent intracranial disease.

renal-flank-pain.S:
CC: Dysuria for 2 days, right flank pain for 1 day.
HPI: 24-year-old woman with worsening constant dull right flank pain just under the ribs, radiating toward groin, 7/10 (8/10 worst); burning on voiding 5/10. Movement/jarring worsen pain; heat/ibuprofen partly help. Fever, shaking chills, nausea, one emesis, frequency, urgency and cloudy malodorous urine; no gross hematuria. Prior bladder infection 6 months ago without flank symptoms. Tried ibuprofen, cranberry juice and fluids. Concerned about kidney damage because aunt required dialysis.
PMH: No chronic conditions. PSH: Wisdom teeth at 18; no admission.
Meds: Oral contraceptive daily; ibuprofen 400 mg a couple times/day for 2 days. Sulfonamides cause hives.
SH: Graduate student; lives with husband off campus; no tobacco/drugs; 2–3 drinks on weekends. One male sexual partner; inconsistent condoms, no new partner. LMP 3 weeks ago, regular; pregnancy possible.
FH: Mother HTN, father diabetes; brother healthy. No known kidney disease/stones in parents/brother; aunt's dialysis cause unknown.
ROS: GU as above, no discharge. GI: nausea/vomiting, no diarrhea/constipation. General: fever/chills, no weight loss. No cough, chest pain, rash or headache.
P: 1. Obtain urine culture/urinalysis, pregnancy test, CBC and BMP; assess intake, perfusion and obstruction/sepsis risk. Clinician to select a renal-tissue-active antibiotic using pregnancy, allergy and resistance data; avoid sulfonamide allergen and nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis. Explain adherence, hydration and urgent deterioration precautions. Emergency evaluation for instability, inability to retain fluids or infected obstruction; otherwise review in 48–72 hours with culture results.

2. Obtain appropriate renal imaging if obstruction is suspected; clinician-directed analgesia/antiemetic and urgent urology input for infected obstruction. Explain that fever with obstruction needs more than hydration.

3. Pregnancy testing and urgent pelvic ultrasound/Doppler if torsion remains suspected; prompt gynecology review without relying on normal Doppler to exclude it. Provide clinician-directed analgesia and explain emergency return for sudden severe pelvic pain.
